newsitem.title: USA: Centennial fires CEO, hires replacement, to restate earnings. [CORRECTED 23:00 gmt]
newsitem.headline: Centennial fires CEO, hires replacement, to restate earnings. [CORRECTED 23:00 gmt]

text.p: Centennial Technologies Inc., last year's best performer on the New York Stock Exchange, said on Tuesday announced plans to restate its recent earnings as the computer card maker's former CEO remained in federal custody after a detention hearing on charges of insider trading.
(Deletes reference to day of arrest, which is corrected in fourth graf).
Centennial, a personal computer card maker, also said it hired an interim chief executive and chief financial officer to replace Emanuel Pinez, who was arrested Friday.
Pinez, 59, an Israeli citizen who has homes in Canada, Switzerland and Beverly and Burlington, Mass., remained in federal custody on Tuesday after a detention hearing.
The company said it faces at least 14 lawsuits by purchasers of its securities from Aug. 21, 1996 through Feb. 11, 1997.
Centennial's stock, which had soared 450 percent during the year to a high of $58.25, plunged $13.50 to $2.875 on the New York Stock Exchange in late trading.
The stock had been halted since Feb. 11, when Centennial announced that previous financial statements had included material misstatements.
Centennial said Lawrence Ramaekers of Boca Raton, Fla., has assumed the post of CEO and Eugene M. Bullis of West Newbury, Mass., has become CFO.

U.S. Magistrate Lawrence Cohen heard in a cramped courtroom that Centennial would restate its earnings for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1996, as well as the first two quarters of fiscal year 1997 and would show the company posting losses in excess of $10 million, more than the amount the computer card maker first reported gaining.
As the litany of fiscal failures continued, Pinez sat in the spectators' first row shaking his head of gray hair.

Looking tired beneath a tan, Pinez, who has a wife in Switzerland, a home in Montreal and two houses and another family in Massachusetts, learned he would face at least three years in prison if convicted of the charges, which include insider trading, overstating revenue and manipulating inventory.

FBI agent Robert Turgiss testified at the detention hearing that Pinez owed Lehman Bros and PaineWebber Group Inc. more than $20 million borrowed "on margin" based on the market value of the stock in his accounts. The stock was primarily shares in Centennial.

His lawyer, Robert Ullmann, attempted to argue that put and call options for Centennial stock, which Pinez began buying three days before he was fired on Feb. 10, were done not at his client's request but because of pressure from the two firms.
But Judge Cohen cut him off, saying, "This is not La-La land. This is not O.J... I will assume unless there is evidence to the contrary that the puts and calls were done by Mr. Pinez."

The Securities and Exchange Commission, in a separate case, has charged that Pinez stands to gain $447,500 from the 2,400 "call" option contracts he bought on Centennial stock. The SEC said the value of the 1,955 "put" options, which expire March 21, could not yet be determined.
"If the value of Centennial stock went down, Mr. Pinez would gain, is that correct?" Judge Cohen asked Turgiss, who replied, "The further Centennial declines, the more Mr. Pinez earns."

But it is unclear if Pinez, or any other Centennial investor, will have a chance to earn any money from the stock. The New York Stock Exchange, which halted trading in the stock Feb. 11, said Tuesday it will suspend trading of the common stock on March 3 and apply to federal regulators to delist it.
The magistrate did not rule on bail and until he does, Pinez will remain in custody.
